# The price of money

## A bond is a promise with a date on it

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Coupon]{.card-title}

Fixed cash on fixed dates. Contractual, not discretionary.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Principal]{.card-title}

Face value, repaid at maturity.
:::

::: {.card}
[Yield]{.card-title}

Not a promise. The rate that makes today's price equal the discounted promises.
:::
:::

## One rate is not enough

$$P = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+r_t)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+r_T)^T}$$

Each cash flow is discounted at the rate for its own maturity. The set of rates
$r_1, \ldots, r_T$ is the term structure.

# When rates move

## Interest rate risk

A bond's price falls when yields rise. The size of the fall depends on the
timing of the cash flows, not on maturity alone.

A 10-year 8% coupon bond returns cash earlier than a 10-year zero, and its price
moves less for the same change in yield.

## Duration {.plain-title}

$$D = \frac{\sum_t t \cdot w_t}{\sum_t w_t}, \qquad w_t = \frac{CF_t}{(1+y)^t}$$

The average date on which you get your money, weighted by present value.

$$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -\frac{D}{1+y} \times \Delta y$$

## Lab 2 — predict, then check {.band-bottom}

::: {.steps}
1. Compute the bond's duration from the same spreadsheet
2. Predict the price change for a 100 bp rise, using $-D^* \times \Delta y$
3. Reprice at the higher yields and compare
:::

::: {.note}
Post two numbers: the predicted price change and the actual one.
:::

## Accuracy of the approximation

The formula is a first-order approximation: it uses the slope of the price-yield
relation at the current yield.

The price-yield relation is convex, so the actual price exceeds the linear
estimate for both increases and decreases in yield. The error grows with the
size of the yield change.
